title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: A Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from a single hosted LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms), declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini, adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with up to one validator‑triggered repair permitted in the guarded arm. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All paired episodes completed (planned episodes = 480; completed = 480; model_calls_used = 240). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change outcomes via validator failure of the single shared generation or via a validator‑triggered repair; validator traces show every shared candidate passed and repair_attempts = 0, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, exact mapping to archived analysis artifacts, diagnostics that explain the degenerate outcome, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into device configurations with minimal human intervention is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible configuration sequences, but text‑level correctness does not ensure safe execution in multi‑device, stateful environments: ordering, transient dependencies, and protected fields create semantic hazards that only an execution‑grounded test can reveal [1]. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipelines—LLM generation followed by deterministic verification and automated repair—are widely proposed to mitigate such hazards, yet empirical evidence about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts is limited and sensitive to experimental design choices [2,3,4].

We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded study whose single estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM output per task reused across both arms). Our run produced a degenerate paired outcome (no discordant pairs). This paper (1) documents the exact preregistered estimand and analysis mapping to archived artifacts, (2) presents the execution accounting and quantitative results, and (3) provides an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining why the guarded pipeline could not produce a contrasting outcome in this run and gives concrete design recommendations for future informative evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks reveal multi‑step and execution semantics failures that text‑only evaluations miss; NetConfArena is one such benchmark that motivated our experimental scope [1]. Generate–validate patterns are well established in program repair and configuration repair literature; prior work demonstrates substantial gains when verifiers catch syntactic and many semantic faults, but success depends on verifier expressiveness and repair search strategy [2,4]. Tool‑augmented agent patterns (self‑critique, tool use, verifier gating) are advocated across agentic NetOps and AIOps research as mechanisms to improve multi‑step correctness and reduce hallucination impact [3,5]. Incremental configuration verification systems (Batfish and follow‑on work) provide engineering precedent for verifier design and for integrating static checks into configuration pipelines [6].

Our study sits at the intersection of these literatures but differs in three ways: (a) we preregistered a single, paired estimand and executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics so paired outcomes are precisely defined by the contract; (b) we used deterministic emulation to assign binary safe/unsafe outcomes; and (c) we archived per‑call provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the measured estimand can be reconciled exactly to immutable artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when executed in the emulator. Analysis parameters (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and the mapping from archived fields to the estimand were fixed in the preregistration and implemented by the registered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Execution contract and generation semantics: We used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused across both baseline and guarded episodes; guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. The requested model was declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini and the deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, paired differences can only arise if (A) the single shared candidate fails deterministic validation (validator reports invalid), or (B) the guarded arm invokes a validator‑triggered repair and replaces the final configuration.

Task corpus and sampling: N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were deterministically generated (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and blocked into topology/vendor clusters. Composition: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48, adversarial‑prompt = 48. The paired design executed each task under both baseline and guarded conditions using the same shared_initial candidate.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator plus validator assigned a binary final outcome: safe (success) or unsafe (failure). Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe_apply) and irrecoverable infra failures after retries; both were to be handled in sensitivity analyses. The retry policy allowed up to two infra retries.

Statistical analysis: The registered analysis executor produced the paired contingency table, a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs. Secondary planned outputs (unused here) included median repair counts and per‑task model call budgets. All parameter values, seeds, and analysis logs are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per preregistered plan. planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; complete_pair_count = 240. Provider call audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and cache_miss_count = 240, consistent with one shared initial generation per task and no additional independent generation calls. model_calls_used = 240 and no infra failures or unscorable episodes occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summaries: baseline_success_count = 240, guarded_success_count = 240. Paired contingency table: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The registered analysis executor output these values deterministically; archived CSVs and logs (condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis_log.jsonl) contain the same numbers.

Validator/repair diagnostics: Validator traces for each episode record validation_before and validation_after snapshots and show validator PASS semantics in every task: violation_count = 0, valid = true. repair_attempts = 0 across the repair logs. The deterministic_reconciliation.json records provider_call_audit.stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240 and all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true, confirming contract adherence and that the guarded arm did not (and could not) exercise repairs on any shared candidate.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only produce discordant pairs if the single shared initial candidate either fails deterministic validation or if the validator triggers (and the guarded adapter applies) a repair that changes the final configuration relative to baseline. In this run every shared candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and no repairs were invoked; therefore no discordant pairs were possible and the paired contrast is degenerate. This diagnosis is drawn directly from archived provider_call_audit, validator traces, and repair logs.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics guarantees a directly paired LLM sample and reduces model‑call budget, but it also prevents evaluation of verifier benefit when generator variability is a realistic source of faults. When the initial generator rarely produces invalid candidates (as here), a paired test under shared_initial_candidate cannot detect verifier benefit. To obtain informative paired contrasts for verifier effectiveness, experimenters should consider (a) permitting independent initial generations per arm so the guarded pipeline can benefit from different generator draws, (b) increasing adversary strength or using adaptive adversaries that are more likely to induce invalid initial candidates, or (c) expanding the repair budget and repair search strategy so the repair machinery can be exercised when validation fails. These recommendations are directly motivated by the archived diagnostics (shared_initial_generation = 240, repair_attempts = 0).

Threats to validity: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract intentionally restricts the causal contrast; our conclusions are conditional on that contract and not general statements about all GVR deployments. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite rule set—validator PASS does not imply exhaustion of all semantic fault classes; planned false‑safe detection checks exist but were not triggered here. External validity: tasks derive from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus and deterministic task generator; extrapolation to diverse production multi‑vendor deployments is limited. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detection of any verifier benefit under the executed design; power calculations in the preregistration assumed larger baseline rates and/or generator variability for informative contrasts.

Operational interpretation: The executed pipeline and verifier succeeded on the supplied synthetic corpus and threat model, but this single‑model, single‑contract result does not imply general verifier superiority or production readiness. Our artifact archive enables the community to reproduce the exact measured estimand and to re‑execute with alternate generation semantics, adversary protocols, or repair budgets to obtain nondegenerate contrasts.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline using a hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Artifact‑grounded diagnostics (provider_call_audit, validator traces, and repair logs) show every shared initial candidate passed validation and repair_attempts = 0; therefore the guarded arm had no opportunity to produce discordant, safer outcomes. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations (allow independent generation per arm, increase adversary strength, expand repair budgets, and extend verifier coverage) for future studies that seek informative paired contrasts. The full preregistration, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived for audit and reanalysis.

Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
